title: Lawmakers decry White House, DOGE ‘witch hunt’ against federal workers
summary: Members of Maryland’s congressional delegation decried the “witch hunt” against federal workers by President Donald Trump and Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency, and vowed to keep fighting for civil servants.
content:
by Jack Bowman, Maryland Matters February 19, 2025

by Jack Bowman, Maryland Matters February 19, 2025

Members of Maryland’s congressional delegation decried the “witch hunt” against federal workers by President Donald Trump and Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency, and vowed to keep fighting for civil servants.

“Elon Musk and his band of misfit, post-pubescent betrayers of America and computer hackers are not opponents of corruption,” Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-8th) said, to a hearty cheer from the audience. “They are agents of corruption,”

His comments came during an hourlong town hall in Silver Spring with Maryland Democratic Sens. Chris Van Hollen and Angela Alsobrooks that was attended by several hundred people, including many civil servants worried about their jobs.

During the campaign, Trump promised the slash the size of federal government, and he created DOGE and appointed tech billionaire Musk to lead the effort. Since Trump’s inauguration a month ago, they have made good on that promise, seeking worker buyouts and aggressively cutting jobs across the board at certain agencies.

It is unclear how many people in Maryland, let alone across the United States, have been swept up in the workforce cuts. But the reductions could disproportionately affect Maryland, which is home to roughly 160,000 federal workers.

Federal workforce hit by Trump’s sweeping firings of thousands of probationary employees

Democrats are quick to pin the plight of federal workers on the White House and the Republican Party, Maryland Republicans say the situation is more complex.

Del. Jesse Pippy (R-Frederick) said that one reason the state may feel workforce cuts more acutely than other states is because of its dependence on the federal government.

“There’s certainly an overreliance,” Pippy said Wednesday morning. “Virginia, other neighboring states to D.C. have done a much better job at diversifying their economy, and they are not over-relying on the federal government.”

But speakers at the Silver Spring event laid the blame for the cuts, and other policies being implemented, at the feet of Trump and Republicans in Congress.

“I keep hearing people say, ‘What are the Democrats going to do?’ The people who at this moment, to me, are complicit are the Republicans,” Alsobrooks said. “They fall right in line, and they have to also begin to be accountable for what is happening now.”

One feature of the administration’s spending and workforce cuts has been targeting probationary employees for layoff. Raskin said he “must have talked to a dozen” such employees who said they had been let go.

“For the vast majority of them, do you know why they’re on probation?” Raskin asked the crowd. “Because they got a promotion. They did so well in their job they got a promotion to a new job, but that put them in a probationary status, and then Elon Musk pounced on that.”

Van Hollen said the firings are not just a matter of policy, he believes they are also illegal.

“What they’re doing is a total violation of their due process rights,” Van Hollen said in an interview before the town hall.

Van Hollen went on to explain that federal employees can only be laid off for performance reasons or for misconduct, and these cuts do not match those criteria.

“You’re seeing some of these letters say to employees that they’re being terminated because of performance when we know that’s a big lie,” Van Hollen said.

Maryland’s senior senator also promised those at the town hall that, while there is no immediate solution, Democrats are working to return people to their jobs, exploring legal options and “using all of our procedural tools.”

“When people get laid off, they should know… we are going to fight to get them fully reinstated with all their protections,” Van Hollen said. “And I think we have a very reasonable chance in many of these cases, if not all of these cases.”
